Verification time stamps were accurate to within one minute in 99 percent of cases. The time of successful read-back was missing in 6 percent of logged calls, usually when the technologist completed the call record later. Collection times were unreliable for community specimens. We recommend measuring notification from verification to documented read-back, treating a missing read-back time as an unsuccessful notification in the primary analysis, and reporting how often end times are missing."},{"title":"Night-shift workload and delays in critical value notification in a hospital laboratory network","authors":"Lindgren-Oyelowo F, Pacheco-Brandt H","year":2023,"venue":"Caddisford Laboratory Practice Journal","doi":"10.5555/jlmp.2023.0207","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Using two years of call logs from a three-hospital network, we examined whether notification delays were linked to night-shift staffing. When a single technologist covered both bench work and notification, the odds of a delay beyond 30 minutes were 2.1 times higher than when a second staff member was available (95 percent CI 1.7 to 2.6), after adjustment for patient location and analyte. Delays clustered in the first hour after large analyser runs. The authors suggest separating notification from bench work at night or routing night calls through a central clinical desk."}]}
